planting.note: Divide rooted rhizome offsets in spring and pot into well-drained mix in medium to bright indirect light; keep this patented selection out of direct sun, especially in hot southern exposures, to avoid scorching the colorful new growth.

directions: Chameleon is a Costa Farms selection of the standard ZZ plant notable for new leaflets that emerge a bright golden-yellow before gradually darkening to deep glossy green, giving each stem a two-tone, color-shifting effect as it matures. It grows into a large, dramatic floor plant over time, eventually reaching several feet tall, yet retains the thick, water-storing rhizomes and general toughness that make ZZ plants nearly indestructible houseplants. Grow in medium to bright indirect light for the clearest gold coloring on new growth, since low light mutes the contrast and strong direct sun can bleach or burn emerging leaflets. Let the potting mix dry out significantly between waterings, since the fleshy rhizomes are highly prone to rot in soggy soil.

planting.note: Divide rooted rhizome offsets in spring and pot into well-drained mix; this patented color-shifting selection needs no special humidity and performs well in typical household conditions.

directions: ZZEverlasting is a patented Brazilian-bred ZZ plant selection whose new leaflets open a vivid lime-green and gradually deepen through darker greens toward a near-black tone as they age, so a single stem can show several shades of color at once. Like other ZZ plants it tolerates average household humidity and temperatures without special care, making it a forgiving choice for beginners and offices. It stores water in its thick, potato-like rhizomes and leaf bases, so it comfortably withstands irregular watering and should be allowed to dry out well between waterings. Provide low to bright indirect light; it tolerates shade but develops its best color contrast with somewhat brighter light.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; this compact selection is especially prone to rot if overwatered, so let the mix dry fully before watering again.

directions: Futura Superba Green is a compact snake plant variety grown by Costa Farms, bearing the same dark green horizontal leaf banding as classic snake plant but on shorter, broader leaves arranged in a tighter rosette than the tall standard forms. Its smaller stature fits desks, shelves, and dish gardens where a full-size upright snake plant would be too large. Like all Dracaena trifasciata forms it is highly tolerant of low light and infrequent watering, but it is far more often killed by overwatering than by neglect, so err on the side of letting the fast-draining mix dry out completely between waterings. Avoid cold drafts and temperatures below the mid-50s Fahrenheit.

planting.note: Root individual leaf-cutting sections or divide offsets in spring, then pot into fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type mix in bright indirect light; this tall variety reaches 1 to 2 feet and suits a sturdy upright container.

directions: Golden Flame is an upright snake plant variety reaching one to two feet tall, with stiff, pointed leaves that carry the gold-and-green variegated coloring suggested by its name along an otherwise classic snake-plant silhouette. It propagates readily from rooted leaf-cutting sections, though variegated color can be inconsistent or lost entirely from leaf cuttings compared with division of rooted offsets. Grow in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix, and water only once the soil has dried out completely, since overwatering is the most common cause of rot in this and other snake plant varieties. It tolerates low light and general neglect well, making it suitable for offices and low-maintenance interiors.

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets in spring and pot into fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type mix in bright indirect light; Black Robusta's deep green, strongly contrasted leaves make it a good accent among lighter-leaved snake plant varieties.

directions: Black Robusta is a snake plant variety grown for its deep, saturated green leaves held in strong contrast against the paler banding typical of the species, giving it a bolder, more dramatic look than standard green forms. It shares the stiff, upright, strap-shaped leaf habit common to Dracaena trifasciata and works well as an architectural accent in a mixed houseplant collection. Grow in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix, watering only after the soil has dried out completely, since this variety rots quickly in wet conditions. It tolerates considerable neglect and lower light once established, though leaf color is richest with brighter indirect light.

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets in spring and pot into fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type mix in bright indirect light; this silvery-leaved compact form suits small pots, dish gardens, and tabletop planting.

directions: White Snow Superba is a compact snake plant variety whose broad leaves carry a pale silver-to-gray overall coloring, a softer, frostier look than the bolder green-and-dark-band patterns typical of the species. Its shorter stature places it among the more compact snake plant selections suited to small containers or grouped dish-garden displays alongside other dwarf forms. Grow in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix, allowing the soil to dry out completely before watering again, since overwatering is by far the most common cause of decline. It tolerates low light and infrequent care well, though the silvery leaf tone is most vivid with consistently bright indirect light.

planting.note: Divide an established clump in spring and pot into humus-rich, moisture-retentive mix in bright indirect light to shade; this Boston fern relative has finer, more lacy frond texture than the standard species.

directions: Green Fantasy is a Boston fern selection with more finely divided, feathery fronds than the standard species, giving it a softer, lacier texture that works especially well in hanging baskets or dish gardens. It shares the same creeping rhizome growth habit as other Nephrolepis exaltata forms and spreads gradually to fill a container with dense, arching fronds. Grow in bright indirect light to shade and keep the humus-rich mix evenly moist, since ferns decline quickly if allowed to dry out completely, while also benefiting from higher humidity such as a bathroom or kitchen setting. Trim off any browned or damaged fronds at the base to keep the plant looking fresh.

planting.note: Divide an established clump in spring and pot into light, humus-rich, moisture-retentive mix in bright indirect light to shade; new fronds emerge with a distinctive pink-rose flush before maturing to green.

directions: Rosy Maidenhair is a maidenhair fern selection prized for new fronds that emerge in rosy-pink tones before maturing to the typical delicate, fan-shaped green leaflets on fine, dark, wiry stems characteristic of Adiantum. Like other maidenhair ferns it is more demanding than tougher houseplant ferns, wanting consistently moist (never soggy) soil, high humidity, and protection from direct sun and drafts. Grow in bright indirect light to shade in a light, humus-rich, well-drained mix, and mist regularly or set the pot on a pebble humidity tray to prevent the thin fronds from crisping in dry indoor air. Trim spent fronds at the base to encourage fresh rosy growth.

planting.note: Divide tuberous rhizome offsets in spring and pot into humus-rich, well-drained mix in bright indirect light to shade; this selection holds a brighter chartreuse-yellow frond color than the plain species.

directions: Lucky Lemon is a selection of the tuberous sword fern grown for its bright chartreuse-to-yellow fronds, a more vivid, sunnier color than the plain green of the species and of other sword fern cultivars. It forms the same small water-storing tubers along its spreading rhizomes as its parent species, which help it tolerate brief dry spells better than many other ferns. Grow in bright indirect light to shade in humus-rich, well-drained mix, keeping the soil evenly moist during active growth while allowing it to dry slightly between waterings to protect the tuberous roots from rot. It spreads readily and works well as a hanging-basket subject or groundcover in frost-free shaded gardens.

planting.note: Mount divisions on bark or pot into a coarse, fast-draining, bark-based epiphytic mix in bright indirect light to shade; the thick, furry rhizomes should stay partly exposed above the growing medium.

directions: Bear Paw fern is an epiphytic species named for its thick, furry, pale rhizomes that creep across the surface of its growing medium like a row of paws, topped by deeply lobed, leathery dark-green fronds. In its native range it grows attached to trees or rocks, so it does best in a coarse, fast-draining, bark-based mix or mounted on a slab rather than buried in dense potting soil. Grow in bright indirect light to shade and water enough to keep the mix lightly moist without letting the furry rhizome sit in standing water, since constant wetness encourages rot. Increase humidity where possible, as this fern is markedly less drought-tolerant than tougher houseplant ferns like Boston or sword fern.
